hints: Sort Period 3 into metals on the left, metalloid Si in the middle, and nonmetals P, S, Cl on the right, then recall which bonding type each group uses as elements.
walkthrough:
Picture the three blocks of Period 3**
Think of $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$ and $\text{Al}$ as metals with a sea of delocalised electrons around positive ions, so they are all M. $\text{Si}$ is a giant covalent network, and $\text{P}$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{Cl}$ exist as simple covalent molecules ($\text{P}_4$, $\text{S}_8$, $\text{Cl}_2$), so they are all C. No element here exists as isolated ions, so I is not used.

Final answer: Z 12 = M, 13 = M, 14 = C, 15 = C, 16 = C
Full row: M M M C C C C

hints: Compare $\text{Na}$ (Z = 11) and $\text{Cl}$ (Z = 17) for number of protons and for number of inner shells shielding the outer electron.
Link the balance of extra protons with almost unchanged shielding to the pull felt by the 3s or 3p electron being removed.
walkthrough:
Count what pulls and what blocks**
First ionisation energy measures how hard it is to pull the outer electron away: $\text{X(g)} \rightarrow \text{X}^{+}\text{(g)} + e^{-}$. Going from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Cl}$ you add 6 protons, so nuclear charge rises a lot. Both atoms remove an n = 3 electron shielded by the 1s, 2s and 2p inner electrons, so shielding stays almost the same.

Feel the stronger net pull**
With more protons pulling and almost no extra shielding to cancel it, the effective nuclear attraction on the outer electron is much larger for $\text{Cl}$. That electron is held tighter, so its removal needs far more energy, $1260$ compared with $494$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: $\text{Cl}$ has greater nuclear charge / more protons than $\text{Na}$.
Shielding is very similar as both outer electrons are in n = 3 shielded by the same inner shells.
Outer electrons are attracted more strongly to the nucleus in $\text{Cl}$, so more energy is needed to remove the first electron.

hints: Write the 3p electron arrangements for $\text{P}$ ($3s^2 3p^3$) and $\text{S}$ ($3s^2 3p^4$) and spot which one first contains a paired box.
Think about what extra repulsion exists when two electrons share the same 3p orbital and how that affects ease of removal.
walkthrough:
Draw the 3p boxes in your head**
$\text{P}$ is $\text{[Ne]} 3s^2 3p^3$ with one electron in each of the three 3p orbitals. $\text{S}$ is $\text{[Ne]} 3s^2 3p^4$, so one 3p orbital now holds a pair. Normally IE rises with proton number, so this drop needs a special reason.

Let the pair push itself out**
Two negative electrons forced into the same small 3p orbital repel each other strongly. This spin-pair repulsion pushes the energy of that paired electron up, so it takes less external energy to remove it from $\text{S}$ than to remove an unpaired electron from the stable half filled shell in $\text{P}$.

Final answer: $\text{S}$ has a spin-paired pair of electrons in a 3p orbital whereas $\text{P}$ has three unpaired 3p electrons.
Repulsion between the paired electrons in the same 3p orbital in $\text{S}$ makes the electron easier to remove, so first IE falls from P to S.

hints: Recall that maximum oxidation number in Period 3 equals the number of outer shell electrons that can be lost or shared, rising by one each step to +7 for Cl.
walkthrough:
Count the outer electrons you can use**
Maximum oxidation number simply counts all $3s$ plus $3p$ valence electrons. $\text{Na}$ can lose 1 to give +1, $\text{Mg}$ can lose 2 to give +2, and so on up to $\text{S}$ giving +6. That fits perfectly with $\text{Cl}$ given as +7.

hints: Check the charges needed to get a noble gas octet: $\text{Si}^{4-}$, $\text{P}^{3-}$, $\text{S}^{2-}$, $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and count electrons in each.
Think what happens to the pull on that fixed set of electrons as proton number rises from 14 to 17.
walkthrough:
Spot the identical electron count**
Each of these ions gains electrons to reach the argon configuration, so $\text{Si}^{4-}$, $\text{P}^{3-}$, $\text{S}^{2-}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ all have 18 electrons. Same electrons, same shells, same shielding.

Add protons to the same cloud**
Moving from $\text{Si}$ (14 protons) to $\text{Cl}$ (17 protons) you squeeze that identical 18 electron cloud with more and more positive charge. Stronger nuclear attraction draws the outer shell in closer, so the anionic radius shrinks steadily.

Final answer: The anions $\text{Si}^{4-}$, $\text{P}^{3-}$, $\text{S}^{2-}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ all have the same number of electrons / same electronic configuration.
Increasing proton number / nuclear charge pulls the same outer electrons more strongly toward the nucleus, so radius decreases from 0.271 to 0.181 $\text{nm}$.

hints: Recall where the melting point peak occurs in Period 3 and why $\text{Si}$ with its giant covalent lattice is so high.
Trace the shape after Si: sharp drop to P, small rise to S, then fall to Cl, reflecting $\text{P}_4$, $\text{S}_8$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ molecular sizes.
walkthrough:
Climb to the giant structures**
From $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Al}$ melting point rises as metallic bonding gets stronger with more delocalised electrons and smaller, more highly charged ions. It peaks sharply at $\text{Si}$ because you must break strong covalent bonds in a giant network.

Drop to the little molecules**
After $\text{Si}$ you fall steeply to $\text{P}$ because $\text{P}_4$, $\text{S}_8$ and $\text{Cl}_2$ are simple molecules held only by weak London forces. $\text{S}_8$ is bigger than $\text{P}_4$ so S sits slightly higher than P, then Cl with small $\text{Cl}_2$ molecules sits lowest. Sketch that exact up then down zigzag shape.

Final answer: Plot melting point vs Z with peak at Si (14).
Rise from Na to Si, sharp fall to P, slight rise to S, fall to Cl.

hints: For density of Al, look at B (2.34) and Ga (5.91) and choose a value smoothly between them, closer to B.
For cationic radius of Ga, place it between Al (0.050 nm) and In (0.081 nm) allowing for the small d-block contraction effect.
For boiling point of In, place it between Ga (2400 K) and Tl (1460 K) on a falling trend down the group.
walkthrough:
Estimate density of aluminium**
Density generally rises down Group 13. $\text{Al}$ sits between $\text{B}$ at $2.34$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$ and $\text{Ga}$ at $5.91$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$. A sensible interpolation is around $2.7$ $\text{g cm}^{-3}$, safely inside the 2.5 to 5.0 range.

Estimate cationic radius of gallium**
Cation size grows down the group as new shells are added. $\text{Ga}$ lies between $0.050$ $\text{nm}$ for $\text{Al}$ and $0.081$ $\text{nm}$ for $\text{In}$. About $0.060$ to $0.065$ $\text{nm}$ fits the steady increase.

Estimate boiling point of indium**
Boiling point falls down the group after B. $\text{In}$ lies between $2400$ $\text{K}$ for $\text{Ga}$ and $1460$ $\text{K}$ for $\text{Tl}$. About $2000$ $\text{K}$ continues the smooth fall.

Final answer: Density of $_{13}\text{Al}$: e.g. 2.70 $\text{g cm}^{-3}$ (any value 2.5 to 5.0).
Cationic radius of $_{31}\text{Ga}$: e.g. 0.062 $\text{nm}$ (any value 0.055 to 0.075).
Boiling point of $_{49}\text{In}$: e.g. 2000 $\text{K}$ (any value 1500 to 2300).

hints: Use the aluminium analogy: Al in HCl gives $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ plus $\text{H}_{2}$, so apply the same +3 oxidation state to indium.
walkthrough:
Copy the aluminium chemistry**
Group 13 metals form $3+$ ions. Just as $\text{Al}$ gives $\text{AlCl}_{3}$ with hydrochloric acid, $\text{In}$ gives $\text{InCl}_{3}$ in solution, with hydrogen as the colourless gas.

hints: Treat $\text{In}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ like $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ with excess NaOH: it forms a tetrahydroxoindate(III) ion, so balance In, Na, O and H with added water.
walkthrough:
Build the alkaline product**
Amphoteric $\text{In}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ reacts with base just like $\text{Al}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ does to give $\text{NaAl(OH)}_{4}$. Here you get $\text{NaIn(OH)}_{4}$. Balancing gives one $\text{In}_{2}\text{O}_{3}$ with $2\text{NaOH}$ and $3\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to make $2\text{NaIn(OH)}_{4}$, with atoms and charge fully balanced.
Final answer: $\text{In}_{2}\text{O}_{3} + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaIn(OH)}_{4}$

hints: Start from the familiar $\text{Al}_{2}\text{Br}_{6}$ dimer: two In atoms linked by two bridging Br atoms, each In also bonded to two terminal Br atoms.
Remember which bonds are dative: the bridging Br atoms each donate a lone pair to the second In, so mark those two coordinate bonds with arrows.
walkthrough:
Sketch the bridged dimer**
Draw two $\text{In}$ centres side by side. Join them with two $\text{Br}$ bridges above and below to make a central four membered $\text{In}_{2}\text{Br}_{2}$ ring. Then attach two terminal $\text{Br}$ atoms to each $\text{In}$, so each $\text{In}$ is surrounded by four $\text{Br}$ atoms in total.

Show the coordinate bonds**
Each bridging $\text{Br}$ makes one normal covalent bond to one $\text{In}$ and one dative bond to the other $\text{In}$ using a lone pair. Mark those two dative bonds with arrows pointing into the $\text{In}$ atoms, exactly as in gaseous $\text{Al}_{2}\text{Cl}_{6}$ or $\text{Al}_{2}\text{Br}_{6}$.

Final answer: Dimer $\text{In}_{2}\text{Br}_{6}$ with two bridging $\text{Br}$ atoms between the two $\text{In}$ atoms and two terminal $\text{Br}$ on each $\text{In}$.
Two dative covalent bonds from bridging $\text{Br}$ to $\text{In}$ clearly shown (arrows pointing to In).
